title: Professional Frontend State Architecture
readme:
FULL STACK DEVELOPER 2026
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend
Phase 23 - Professional Frontend State Architecture

Purpose:
Assign one authoritative owner to each kind of frontend state. This phase adds no new global state library.

Key owners:
- TanStack Query: server state
- Next.js URL: navigation/filter/pagination state
- React Hook Form: unsaved form state
- Supabase Auth: session identity
- useState/useReducer: local interaction state
- focused Context: justified cross-tree distribution
- derived values: compute, do not duplicate

lessons.title: State Taxonomy and Ownership Decision Framework
lessons.summary: State Taxonomy and Ownership Decision Framework Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 The first question is ownership, not API choice When developers ask "Should this use Context or Zustand?", they often skip the more important question: what kind of information is this, and…
lessons.body:
State Taxonomy and Ownership
Decision Framework
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

The first question is ownership, not API choice
When developers ask "Should this use Context or Zustand?", they often skip the more important
question: what kind of information is this, and which subsystem is already responsible for it?

React documentation emphasizes a single source of truth for each unique piece of state. That does not
mean all application state belongs in one global location; it means each piece has one authoritative
owner.

TaskFlow decision tree

Does it come from the server?

YES                                      NO                                    YES
TanStack Query                    Should the URL preserve it?                     URL state

Is it unsaved form input?               Does only nearby UI need it?

YES                                    YES                                     NO
React Hook Form                      useState/useReducer                  Context only if truly shared

Figure 23.1 - TaskFlow decision tree

Practical matrix
Task rows                   Server state -> TanStack Query. Do not copy them into useState just to render them.

Search + page               URL state -> searchParams/router because navigation, refresh, history, and sharing
should preserve them.

Unsaved title               Form state -> React Hook Form because it owns dirty/touched/errors/submission
semantics.

Mobile menu                 Local UI state -> useState because it is ephemeral and belongs to one interaction
open                        boundary.

Authenticated               Supabase Auth. Other layers consume verified identity; they do not invent a second
session                     session store.

Completed Task             Derived state -> compute from authoritative data instead of storing a second count.
count

Decision rule
Choose the narrowest owner that can correctly preserve the state for the lifetime and scope
it actually needs.

lessons.title: Avoid Redundant Duplicate and Synchronized State
lessons.summary: Avoid Redundant, Duplicate and Synchronized State Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 The most expensive state is copied state Every duplicate introduces a synchronization problem. If a value can be derived from props, query data, URL state, or another state variable during render,…
lessons.body:
Avoid Redundant, Duplicate and
Synchronized State
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

The most expensive state is copied state
Every duplicate introduces a synchronization problem. If a value can be derived from props, query data,
URL state, or another state variable during render, storing another copy usually increases bug surface
without adding capability.

Classic TaskFlow anti-pattern
const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query))

const [tasks, setTasks] = useState<Task[]>([])

useEffect(() => {
if (tasksQuery.data) {
setTasks(tasksQuery.data.data)
}
}, [tasksQuery.data])

Duplication creates synchronization work

Query cache              useEffect          Local state                                Rendered UI
tasks[]                                  tasks[] copy                                 table rows

Better: render directly from the query result unless the user is intentionally editing a draft.

Figure 23.1 - Classic TaskFlow anti-pattern

Better
const tasksQuery = useQuery(taskListOptions(query))

const tasks = tasksQuery.data?.data ?? []

When a copy is legitimate
• The user is editing a draft that must diverge from server data.

• You are taking a deliberate snapshot for undo/history.

• An animation/intermediate interaction needs its own transient representation.

• You have explicitly named the synchronization boundary and its conflict policy.

Effect warning

Do not use an effect merely to keep one state variable equal to another value you already have. Effects
are for synchronizing React with external systems; they are not a general-purpose data copier.

lessons.title: Local UI State useState and Component Ownership
lessons.summary: Local UI State, useState and Component Ownership Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 Keep ephemeral interaction state local Mobile navigation visibility, a disclosure panel, a temporary hover preview, and a non-shareable dialog tab usually belong to the smallest client component that needs them.…
lessons.body:
Local UI State, useState and
Component Ownership
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

Keep ephemeral interaction state local
Mobile navigation visibility, a disclosure panel, a temporary hover preview, and a non-shareable dialog
tab usually belong to the smallest client component that needs them. Moving them to a global store
makes them harder to reason about and couples unrelated parts of the tree.

Example
"use client"

export function MobileNavigation() {
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)

return (
<>
<button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Menu</button>
{open && <MobileMenu onClose={() => setOpen(false)} />}
</>
)
}

When to lift state
If two sibling components must coordinate the same value, move that value to their closest common
owner and pass data/actions downward. Do not immediately jump to Context.

TaskFlow examples
• Table row hover -> row/table component.

• Selected rows for a bulk action -> Task table boundary.

• Shell mobile navigation -> shell client boundary.

• Global toast queue may justify a shared provider because many distant features publish messages.

lessons.title: URL State Filters Pagination and Deep Linkability
lessons.summary: URL State: Filters, Pagination and Deep Linkability Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 The URL is a state container Phase 15 already made Task filters, sorting, and pagination part of the HTTP collection contract. Phase 22 made those values part of query keys.…
lessons.body:
URL State: Filters, Pagination and
Deep Linkability
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

The URL is a state container
Phase 15 already made Task filters, sorting, and pagination part of the HTTP collection contract. Phase
22 made those values part of query keys. Phase 23 completes the model: the browser URL is their
canonical frontend owner.

Why URL ownership matters
• Refresh preserves the view.

• Back/forward navigation behaves naturally.

• A teammate can share the exact filtered screen.

• Server Components can read the same navigation state.

• TanStack Query keys can be built from normalized URL state instead of an unrelated local copy.

Flow
/tasks?status=IN_PROGRESS&page=2&search=payroll
|
v
searchParams -> normalize -> TaskListQuery
|
v
taskKeys.list(query) -> TanStack Query -> NestJS

Client reading
In the current Next.js App Router, useSearchParams() is a Client Component hook that returns a
read-only URLSearchParams view. Pages and Server Components can also receive route search
parameters through the route API. Use the URL as the source, not a second filter object that must be
synchronized.

Reset page intentionally
When search, status, priority, or page size changes, TaskFlow normally resets page=1. This
is a navigation rule, not a query-cache concern.

lessons.title: Form State vs Server State
lessons.summary: Form State vs Server State Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 A form is an intentional divergence from the server This is one of the few places where a local copy is not accidental. Once the user begins editing, the draft is allowed…
lessons.body:
Form State vs Server State
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

A form is an intentional divergence from the server
This is one of the few places where a local copy is not accidental. Once the user begins editing, the draft
is allowed to differ from the last server response. React Hook Form owns that draft until
submission/reset/cancel resolves the divergence.

Do not bind the editor directly to the cache
Server Task (TanStack Query)
|
v
defaultValues / reset()
|
v
React Hook Form draft
| user edits
v
mutateAsync(payload)
|
v
NestJS -> database
|
v
invalidate / update relevant query cache

Conflict awareness
• If the server changes while a dirty form is open, do not silently overwrite the user draft.

• A simple CRUD screen may refresh after successful save.

• Collaborative editing needs a much more explicit conflict/version strategy and belongs to a later
architecture discussion.

Ownership rule
Query data initializes the form. It does not continuously control the form while the user is
editing.

lessons.title: Auth Session Workspace and Cross Tree Context
lessons.summary: Auth, Workspace and Cross-Tree Context Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 Context is a delivery mechanism, not automatically the owner Context is useful when many descendants need the same stable value and prop drilling would obscure the component API. But the value inside…
lessons.body:
Auth, Workspace and Cross-Tree
Context
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

Context is a delivery mechanism, not automatically the
owner
Context is useful when many descendants need the same stable value and prop drilling would obscure
the component API. But the value inside Context should still have a clear authoritative source.

Authentication
• Supabase Auth owns the authenticated session.

• NestJS independently verifies access tokens.

• A React Context may expose convenience data to descendants, but it must not create a second
authentication truth.

Workspace scope
Business scope should remain reconstructable

URL                           Server                         Context                         UI
/w/acme/tasks                 resolve workspace              read resolved info              header/menu

Avoid making a transient Context value the only record of which workspace the user is viewing.

Figure 23.1 - Workspace scope

For a multi-workspace business system, a deep-linkable route such as
/w/[workspaceSlug]/tasks is often a stronger canonical owner than a transient Context-only
selection. Context can then distribute the already-resolved workspace to deep UI children.

Do not put everything in one AppContext
// Avoid a kitchen-sink context
{
user, tasks, filters, page, modalOpen,
formDraft, selectedWorkspace, notifications,
isLoading, error, ...
}

Prefer focused boundaries

• WorkspaceContext -> resolved current workspace metadata.

• Toast/notification provider -> transient cross-tree notifications.

• Theme provider -> presentation preference if the app supports it.

• Do not move query cache, RHF form state, or URL filters into those contexts.

lessons.title: When Context or Global State is Actually Justified
lessons.summary: When Context or Global State Is Actually Justified Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23 Do not ban global state; earn it After moving server state to TanStack Query, forms to React Hook Form, filters to the URL, auth to Supabase, and ephemeral interactions…
lessons.body:
When Context or Global State Is
Actually Justified
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

Do not ban global state; earn it
After moving server state to TanStack Query, forms to React Hook Form, filters to the URL, auth to
Supabase, and ephemeral interactions to local React state, many business applications have surprisingly
little synchronous global client state left.

Good Context candidates
• Resolved workspace metadata consumed across the app shell.

• Theme/preferences that are genuinely cross-tree.

• Toast/notification dispatcher.

• Feature-level state shared by a deep subtree whose owner is still obvious.

When an external client store may become justified
• Large synchronous client-only models shared across distant trees.

• High-frequency cross-feature updates where Context composition becomes unwieldy.

• Offline-first editing queues or complex visual editors.

• State machines with broad client ownership independent of server cache.

TaskFlow decision
Phase 23 adds no Zustand, Redux, MobX, or other global store. There is not yet a problem in
TaskFlow that requires one. Adding one now would teach tool accumulation instead of
architecture.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend | Phase 23

Lab 1 - State inventory
Create an inventory of every stateful value on the Tasks screen. For each value, record category,
authoritative owner, lifetime, reset event, and whether it must survive refresh/navigation.

Lab 2 - Remove one duplicated state path
Find code shaped like:
query data -> useEffect -> useState -> render

Replace it with:
query data -> render

Then verify:
- background refetch updates the table
- pagination still works
- no stale copy remains

Lab 3 - URL-owned filters
• Change status/search/page through navigation.

• Refresh the browser and confirm the same view returns.

• Use browser Back/Forward and confirm the query follows the URL.

• Copy the URL into a new tab and confirm the same collection state is reconstructed.

Lab 4 - Workspace architecture
Design the next routing shape for multi-workspace TaskFlow. Compare a Context-only active workspace
with a route-scoped workspace such as /w/[workspaceSlug]/tasks. Document which state remains
canonical and what Context merely distributes.

Phase exit checklist
• I can classify state before choosing a hook/library.

• I can explain why query data should not normally be copied into local state.

• I can distinguish form draft state from server state.

• I use URL state for shareable navigation state.

• I keep local UI state close to its interaction owner.

• I know when Context is useful and when it is hiding unclear ownership.

• I derive values instead of synchronizing duplicates.

• I can justify adding a new global state library only with a concrete unsolved problem.

Sources used in this phase

Source                                     Why it matters

React - Sharing State Between Components   Single source of truth; lift shared state to the closest common
owner.

React - Managing State                     Avoid redundant/duplicate state; structure state intentionally.

Next.js - useSearchParams                  URL query state in the App Router.

TanStack Query - Query State / Cache       Server-state cache is separate from local UI state.

TanStack Query - SSR/Hydration             Request-scoped QueryClient and cache isolation.

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 23: Professional Frontend State Architecture

Purpose
Choose the correct owner for URL state, server state, local UI state, forms, and global client state instead of duplicating everything.

Deliverable
A state ownership map for TaskFlow plus refactored examples removing redundant synchronized state.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
classify state -> choose authoritative owner -> derive values -> share only when necessary -> avoid synchronization loops

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Inventory every state variable on one TaskFlow screen and classify it: server, URL, form, local UI, or cross-cutting client.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Move filter/search/page state that should survive/share navigation into URL search params.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Remove local copies of TanStack Query data and derive filtered/presentational values during render.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Step 4 — Keep ephemeral dialog/menu state at the smallest component that owns it.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Evaluate whether any global store is actually needed; write the requirement before adding one.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Create a diagram showing source of truth and allowed data flow for the screen.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 23: Professional Frontend State Architecture

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
classify state -> choose authoritative owner -> derive values -> share only when necessary -> avoid synchronization loops

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — useEffect syncing query data into local state
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Global store used for all state categories
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — URL and React state disagreeing about filters
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Storing derived values that can be computed
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.title: Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge
lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 23 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Professional Frontend State Architecture

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 23 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Choose the correct owner for URL state, server state, local UI state, forms, and global client state instead of duplicating everything.

Required artifact
A state ownership map for TaskFlow plus refactored examples removing redundant synchronized state.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can classify state before choosing library.
• Can remove duplicate state.
• Can use URL for shareable navigation state.
• Can justify any global client store.

Independent build sequence
1. Inventory every state variable on one TaskFlow screen and classify it: server, URL, form, local UI, or cross-cutting client.
2. Move filter/search/page state that should survive/share navigation into URL search params.
3. Remove local copies of TanStack Query data and derive filtered/presentational values during render.
4. Keep ephemeral dialog/menu state at the smallest component that owns it.
5. Evaluate whether any global store is actually needed; write the requirement before adding one.
6. Create a diagram showing source of truth and allowed data flow for the screen.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 23: Professional Frontend State Architecture. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
A state ownership map for TaskFlow plus refactored examples removing redundant synchronized state.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

references.preview:
# TaskFlow Phase 23 Reference Snapshot

This snapshot demonstrates state ownership decisions. It is intentionally small and does not add a global state library.

Owners:
- TanStack Query: server state
- Next.js URL: filters/pagination/shareable navigation
- React Hook Form: unsaved form drafts
- Supabase Auth: authentication session
- React local state/reducer: ephemeral UI interaction
- Focused Context: only stable cross-tree convenience values

# Sources

- React - Sharing State Between Components: https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components - Single source of truth; lift shared state to the closest common owner.
- React - Managing State: https://react.dev/learn/managing-state - Avoid redundant/duplicate state; structure state intentionally.
- Next.js - useSearchParams: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params - URL query state in the App Router.
- TanStack Query - Query State / Cache: https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/reference/interfaces/QueryState - Server-state cache is separate from local UI state.
- TanStack Query - SSR/Hydration: https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/ssr - Request-scoped QueryClient and cache isolation.

# TaskFlow State Ownership Matrix

| Value | Owner | Why | Reset / lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Task collection | TanStack Query | Remote server state | Cache freshness/auth lifecycle |
| status/search/page | URL | Shareable navigation | Route change |
| Task edit draft | React Hook Form | Intentional unsaved divergence | reset/cancel/success |
| Supabase session | Supabase Auth | Identity provider owns session | logout/expiry |
| mobile menu open | local useState | Ephemeral shell interaction | close/unmount |
| selected Task rows | local reducer | Feature interaction state | clear/filter/page change |
| current workspace slug | URL route scope | Reconstructable tenant scope | navigation |
| resolved workspace metadata | focused Context | convenient deep distribution | route/workspace change |
| completed count | derived | Calculated from authoritative result | render |

# Phase 23 State Architecture Test Matrix

1. Change status filter -> URL changes, page resets to 1.
2. Refresh -> same filter/page reconstructs.
3. Back/Forward -> collection follows browser history.
4. Background query refetch -> Task table updates without a copied local array.
5. Dirty edit form -> query refetch does not overwrite unsaved draft.
6. Successful save -> form reset + relevant query cache updated/invalidated.
7. Mobile menu -> local interaction only; no global store.
8. Logout -> Query cache cleared; previous user server data not shown.
9. Workspace route change -> resolved workspace Context updates from route/server owner.
10. Derived completed count -> changes automatically with task data, no effect synchronization.
